questions.prompt: Which cast operator should you use to convert a scoped enum class value into its underlying integer type in C++23?
questions.code: enum class Status : std::uint16_t { Ok = 0, Busy = 1 };
options: std::to_underlying(Status::Busy) or static_cast<std::uint16_t>(Status::Busy)
reinterpret_cast<std::uint16_t>(Status::Busy)
const_cast<std::uint16_t>(Status::Busy)
dynamic_cast<std::uint16_t>(Status::Busy)
questions.explanation: Scoped enums do not implicitly convert to integers, so static_cast or C++23 std::to_underlying (which wraps static_cast<std::underlying_type_t<E>>) is the idiomatic, type-safe conversion. reinterpret_cast rejects non-pointer enum-to-int conversions.

questions.prompt: What guarantee does qualifying a variable as volatile provide in multi-threaded C++ code?
options: Atomic reads and writes without tearing
Release/acquire memory ordering across CPU cores
Neither atomicity nor cross-thread ordering; it only prevents compiler access elision and reordering of volatile accesses
Hardware cache-line flushing on every store
questions.explanation: volatile tells the compiler each access is an observable side effect for MMIO or signal handlers, forbidding register caching. It provides zero atomicity or happens-before guarantees across threads; use std::atomic for concurrency.

questions.prompt: Why does the assignment `const int** pp = &p;` fail to compile when `p` has type `int*`, whereas `const int* const* pp = &p;` compiles?
options: Because pointer-to-pointer types never allow implicit qualification conversions
Because converting int** to const int** would let *pp store a const int* into p, enabling mutation of a const object through p without a cast
Because const int* and int* have different sizes and alignments
Because C++ requires reinterpret_cast whenever two pointers differ in cv-qualification
questions.explanation: Under [conv.qual], adding const at an inner pointer level requires every outer level up to the top to also become const. Otherwise *pp = &some_const_int would leave the non-const int* p pointing at a const object.

questions.prompt: What happens when `modify(x)` executes on a variable defined as `const int x = 10;`?
options: x reliably becomes 20 because const_cast removes the reference's constness
Compilation fails because const_cast only accepts pointers, not references
Undefined behavior, because modifying an object that was originally defined const is UB regardless of const_cast
Implementation-defined write that succeeds whenever x has automatic storage duration
questions.explanation: const_cast only removes const from the access path; [dcl.type.cv] states that any attempt to modify an object defined as const through a non-const glvalue results in undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: Given `struct PrivDerived : private Base {};` and `PrivDerived* pd`, how do `static_cast<Base*>(pd)` and `(Base*)pd` differ?
options: Both fail to compile because Base is an inaccessible private base class
static_cast<Base*>(&d) fails to compile, whereas (Base*)&d is well-formed and adjusts the pointer to the private Base subobject
Both succeed and invoke reinterpret_cast without adjusting subobject offsets
static_cast<Base*>(&d) succeeds via friendship rules while (Base*)&d calls reinterpret_cast
questions.explanation: Under [expr.cast], an explicit C-style cast performs the same subobject pointer adjustment as static_cast even when the base class is private or protected—bypassing access checking that static_cast strictly enforces.

questions.prompt: Which technique inspects the bit pattern of a `float` as a `std::uint32_t` without violating `[basic.lval]` strict aliasing rules?
options: auto bits = *reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*>(&f);
union U { float f; std::uint32_t u; } x{f}; auto bits = x.u;
auto bits = *(std::uint32_t*)(void*)&f;
auto bits = std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f);
questions.explanation: Reading a float through a std::uint32_t* via reinterpret_cast or C-style cast violates strict aliasing ([basic.lval]), and reading an inactive union member is UB in C++. std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f) (or std::memcpy) creates a valid std::uint32_t object from the bytes.
